Judgment against divided worship (verses 1–6)

Complete destruction was approaching, brought by the Almighty.

The prophets consistently warned that there is no peace for the wicked.

Their language pictured the devastation of the land in vivid images, as though it would be left without inhabitants.

Those facing judgment included people openly practicing idolatry.

They also included people who claimed to worship Jehovah while worshiping idols, swearing by the Lord and by Malcham.

God will not accept hearts and worship divided between himself and false gods.

What fellowship can there be between light and darkness?

If Satan receives half of our allegiance, he will demand all of it.

If the Lord receives only half, he will accept none of it.

Neglecting God is itself an expression of irreverence and contempt.

May we not belong to those who turn away and perish, but to those who believe and receive the salvation of their souls.

Pride, oppression and indifference judged (verses 7–13)

The day appointed by the Lord was near.

The punishment of presumptuous sinners would be like a sacrifice offered to divine justice.

The royal household of Judah would have to answer for pride and vanity.

Others would answer for leaping over the threshold to invade their neighbors' rights and seize their belongings.

Traders and rich merchants would also be called to account.

The Lord would confront the comfortable and indifferent.

They believed themselves secure and said in their hearts that the Lord would neither do good nor do harm.

In effect they denied that God rewards righteousness or punishes evil.

But the day of his judgment would show that people perish for breaking his law and because they lack, through faith, any share in the Redeemer's atoning sacrifice.

The terrifying day of the Lord (verses 14–18)

The warning of approaching destruction was enough to make even sinners in Zion tremble.

The day of the Lord would reveal his anger through the punishment of evil.

It was near—a day of wrath, trouble and distress for sinners.

We must not allow God's patience to lull us into false security.

What does a person gain by obtaining the whole world if that person loses their soul?

And what can anyone give in exchange for the soul?

Let us flee from the wrath to come and choose the good portion that can never be taken away.

Then we will be ready for whatever happens.

Nothing will separate us from God's love in Christ Jesus our Lord.
classic_reading:
[Zeph.1.1-Zeph.1.6]
Zephaniah
Zephaniah excites to repentance, foretells the destruction of the enemies of the Jews, and comforts the pious among them with promises of future blessings, the restoration of their nation, and the prosperity of the church in the latter days.
Chapter 1
Chapter Outline
Threatenings against sinners. | (1-6) |
More threatenings. | (7-13) |
Distress from the approaching judgments. | (14-18) |
Verses 1-6
Ruin is coming, utter ruin; destruction from the Almighty. The servants of God all proclaim, There is no peace for the wicked. The expressions are figurative, speaking every where desolation; the land shall be left without inhabitants. The sinners to be consumed are, the professed idolaters, and those that worship Jehovah and idols, or swear to the Lord, and to Malcham. Those that think to divide their affections and worship between God and idols, will come short of acceptance with God; for what communion can there be between light and darkness? If Satan have half, he will have all; if the Lord have but half, he will have none. Neglect of God shows impiety and contempt. May none of us be among those who draw back unto perdition, but of those who believe to the saving of the soul.
[Zeph.1.7-Zeph.1.13]
Verses 7-13
God's day is at hand; the punishment of presumptuous sinners is a sacrifice to the justice of God. The Jewish royal family shall be reckoned with for their pride and vanity; and those that leap on the threshold, invading their neighbours' rights, and seizing their possessions. The trading people and the rich merchants are called to account. Secure and careless people are reckoned with. They are secure and easy; they say in their heart, the Lord will not do good, neither will he do evil; that is, they deny his dispensing rewards and punishments. But in the day of the Lord's judgment, it will clearly appear that those who perish, fall a sacrifice to Divine justice for breaking God's law, and because they have no interest by faith in the Redeemer's atoning sacrifice.
[Zeph.1.14-Zeph.1.18]
Verses 14-18
This warning of approaching destruction, is enough to make the sinners in Zion tremble; it refers to the great day of the Lord, the day in which he will show himself by taking vengeance on them. This day of the Lord is very near; it is a day of God's wrath, wrath to the utmost. It will be a day of trouble and distress to sinners. Let them not be laid asleep by the patience of God. What is a man profited if he gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? And what shall a man give in exchange for his soul? Let us flee from the wrath to come, and choose the good part that shall never be taken from us; then we shall be prepared for every event; nothing shall separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.

Seek the Lord before judgment (verses 1–3)

The prophet called his nation to repentance as the only means of preventing national destruction.

One description of this people could mean a nation without desire: people who did not desire God, his favor or his grace and were unwilling to repent or reform.

It could also mean a nation without anything desirable: people who had nothing in themselves to recommend them to God.

He might justly have told them to leave his presence.

Instead he called them to gather before him and seek his face.

We know what his decree brings upon people who persist in sin.

Therefore everyone has urgent reason to repent while the opportunity to receive grace remains.

Seek peace with God now, before the Holy Spirit ceases striving with you, before the day of grace or of earthly life is over, and before your everlasting condition has been determined.

Let the poor, despised and afflicted seek the Lord.

Let them seek to understand and obey his commands more faithfully and grow more humble over their sins.

The greatest hope of deliverance from national judgments lies in prayer.

Judgment on neighboring nations (verses 4–15)

People are in a truly dreadful position when the word of the Lord announces judgment against them.

Not one of his words will fail.

God will restore his people to what rightfully belongs to them, even after they have been deprived of it for a long time.

In every age, people devoted to God have commonly faced mockery and abuse.

Yet God will be worshiped not only by Israel and the strangers who join it, but also by people from the nations.

Even distant peoples will be called to account for the wrongs they have done to his people.

When those who were arrogant and cruel in their prosperity suffer, others may offer them neither sympathy nor lament.

The destruction of once-flourishing nations will nonetheless prepare the way for the overthrow of Satan's kingdom.

Let us use the advantages God has given us well.

Let us expect him to fulfill every promise.

And let us pray that our Father's name will be honored and made holy throughout the earth.

[Zeph.2.1-Zeph.2.3]
Chapter 2
Chapter Outline
An exhortation to repentance. | (1-3) |
Judgments upon other nations. | (4-15) |
Verses 1-3
The prophet calls to national repentance, as the only way to prevent national ruin. A nation not desiring, that has not desires toward God, is not desirous of his favour and grace, has no mind to repent and reform. Or, not desirable, not having any thing to recommend them to God; to whom God might justly say, Depart from me; but he says, Gather together to me that you may seek my face. We know what God's decree will bring against impenitent sinners, therefore it highly concerns all to repent in the accepted time. How careful should we all be to seek peace with God, before the Holy Spirit withdraws from us, or ceases to strive with us; before the day of grace is over, or the day of life; before our everlasting state is determined! Let the poor, despised, and afflicted, seek the Lord, and seek to understand and keep his commandments better, that they may be more humbled for their sins. The chief hope of deliverance from national judgments rests upon prayer.
[Zeph.2.4-Zeph.2.15]
Verses 4-15
Those are really in a woful condition who have the word of the Lord against them, for no word of his shall fall to the ground. God will restore his people to their rights, though long kept from them. It has been the common lot of God's people, in all ages, to be reproached and reviled. God shall be worshipped, not only by all Israel, and the strangers who join them, but by the heathen. Remote nations must be reckoned with for the wrongs done to God's people. The sufferings of the insolent and haughty in prosperity, are unpitied and unlamented. But all the desolations of flourishing nations will make way for the overturning Satan's kingdom. Let us improve our advantages, and expect the performance of every promise, praying that our Father's name may be hallowed every where, over all the earth.

Further reproof for sin (verses 1–7)

The holy God hates sin most severely when it is committed by those who live nearest to him and enjoy the greatest spiritual privileges.

A people living in sin already occupies a miserable position and will face misery if they do not repent.

Judah possessed signs of God's presence and many opportunities to know his will.

These privileges gave its people the strongest reasons to obey him.

Yet they continued in disobedience.

How sad it is that human beings often put more energy into wrongdoing than believers put into doing good!

Mercy, purification and the humble remnant (verses 8–13)

Henry understands this prophecy as looking toward the proclamation of the gospel, even when judgment would fall upon the Jewish nation.

The gospel's purifying teaching—the pure language of the Lord's grace—would teach people to speak and live with humility, repentance and faith.

Clean and godly everyday conversation is itself a good thing.

Henry also sees here a promise of the church's purity and happiness in later days.

The Lord will remove boasting.

He will leave people nothing in which to glory except Jesus Christ, whom God has made their wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption.

Humility about sin and gratitude toward the Redeemer will make real believers upright and sincere, even when other people profess religion without living accordingly.

Future joy and restoration (verses 14–20)

After promises that sin will be removed come promises that suffering will be removed.

When the cause of trouble is taken away, the resulting distress can finally cease.

What makes God's people holy will make them happy.

The promises given to a purified people find their complete accomplishment in the gospel.

Henry understands these verses principally as referring to the future conversion and restoration of Israel and the glorious days to follow.

He expects the church to experience great peace, comfort and blessing in those times.

He will save.

Jesus fulfills the meaning of his name, for he saves his people from their sins.

Before those promised days, believers may experience great sorrow and suffer disgrace.

But the Lord will rescue even the weakest believer and honor genuine Christians where they were once despised.

In Henry's interpretation, the same act of mercy would gather scattered Israel and lead its people back to their land.

Then God's Israel would receive enduring honor.

Only the fulfillment of events will fully explain the language of the prophecy.

The righteous have many troubles, but they can rejoice in God's love.

How deeply we should honor and rejoice in the Lord when we hear such gracious words!

If we are now unable to take part in his appointed worship, we rightly feel the loss.

But one day we will be gathered into his heavenly temple.

The believer's happiness and glory will be complete, unchanging and eternal when earthly sorrows have ended.
classic_reading:
[Zeph.3.1-Zeph.3.7]
Chapter 3
Chapter Outline
Further reproofs for sin. | (1-7) |
Encouragement to look for mercy. | (8-13) |
Promises of future favour and prosperity. | (14-20) |
Verses 1-7
The holy God hates sin most in those nearest to him. A sinful state is, and will be, a woful state. Yet they had the tokens of God's presence, and all the advantages of knowing his will, with the strongest reasons to do it; still they persisted in disobedience. Alas, that men often are more active in doing wickedness than believers are in doing good.
[Zeph.3.8-Zeph.3.13]
Verses 8-13
The preaching of the gospel is predicted, when vengeance would be executed on the Jewish nation. The purifying doctrines of the gospel, or the pure language of the grace of the Lord, would teach men to use the language of humility, repentance, and faith. Purity and piety in common conversation is good. The pure and happy state of the church in the latter days seems intended. The Lord will shut out boasting, and leave men nothing to glory in, save the Lord Jesus, as made of God to them wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption. Humiliation for sin, and obligations to the Redeemer, will make true believers upright and sincere, whatever may be the case among mere professors.
[Zeph.3.14-Zeph.3.20]
Verses 14-20
After the promises of taking away sin, follow promises of taking away trouble. When the cause is removed, the effect will cease. What makes a people holy, will make them happy. The precious promises made to the purified people, were to have full accomplishment in the gospel. These verses appear chiefly to relate to the future conversion and restoration of Israel, and the glorious times which are to follow. They show the abundant peace, comfort, and prosperity of the church, in the happy times yet to come. He will save; he will be Jesus; he will answer the name, for he will save his people from their sins. Before the glorious times foretold, believers would be sorrowful, and objects of reproach. But the Lord will save the weakest believer, and cause true Christians to be greatly honoured where they had been treated with contempt. One act of mercy and grace shall serve, both to gather Israel out of their dispersions and to lead them to their own land. Then will God's Israel be made a name and a praise to eternity. The events alone can fully answer the language of this prophecy. Many are the troubles of the righteous, but they may rejoice in God's love. Surely our hearts should honour the Lord, and rejoice in him, when we hear such words of condescension and grace. If now kept from his ordinances, it is our trial and grief; but in due time we shall be gathered into his temple above. The glory and happiness of the believer will be perfect, unchangeable, and eternal, when he is freed from earthly sorrows, and brought to heavenly bliss.
